info.desc: "Play" is the sixth studio album by the music artist Moby. While some of Moby's earlier work garnered critical and commercial success within the electronic dance music scene, "Play" was his first true pop success. The album introduced Moby to a worldwide mainstream audience, not only through hit singles, but also through unprecedented licensing of his music in films, television and commercial advertisements. One of the notable aspects of "Play", as opposed to other electronic albums of the time, was the way in which it combined old gospel and folk music rhythms with modern house sensibilities. This unprecedented level of commercial integration made Moby a target for numerous critics who labeled him a "gigantic sellout" for allegedly prostituting his art for financial gain. "Every single song in the play album, and there were 17 tracks in the CD, have been licensed for use in everything from TV shows and movie soundtracks to TV commercials."

podcast.body: Initially released in 1999, *Play* was a commercial failure, selling only a few thousand units in its first days and failing to chart, leading Moby to believe his career was over. To recoup costs, his representative licensed the album's tracks very cheaply for TV commercials, radio ads, and films due to their ambient nature. This strategy led to the album gaining immense popularity, especially in Europe initially, before becoming a global phenomenon and making Moby a millionaire. "movi assume ya que es el final de su carrera no consigue ya después de todo ese trabajo intimista dedicado dos años hípico no da ningún resultado."

podcast.body: Moby and his manager devised a groundbreaking strategy to license all 18 tracks from the "Play" album for TV commercials and shows, as traditional radio and video channels showed little interest. This "licensed everything strategy" proved incredibly successful, leading to weekly sales of 150,000 copies, nine hit singles, all tracks being licensed, and global sales exceeding 10 million copies. The album transformed Moby from a cult DJ into a worldwide star, though some fans criticized the extensive commercialization, exemplified by an attempt to sell his "soul" on eBay. "The album itself sold somewhere north of 10 million copies."

podcast.body: Moby's fifth studio album, released in 1999, became a landmark by offering all 18 of its songs to advertising agencies, film studios, and TV producers. This unprecedented gamble by his management team aimed to expose his music to a wider audience than traditional touring and radio airplay could provide. The strategy proved immensely successful, with companies like Nordstrom, Volkswagen, and Levi's licensing every single track, leading to widespread recognition for Moby and ultimately selling 12 million copies worldwide. It served as a significant "wake-up call" for the artist community, especially as music piracy surged and physical music sales plummeted in the subsequent years. "Every single track was licensed. Everyone heard about Mobie as a result. And play ended up selling 12 million copies."

podcast.body: This album is described as a journey through 50-60 years of music, incorporating gospel, soul, funk, and blues, which was particularly remarkable for an American artist. It introduced a new, more subdued and ambient electronic sound to the United States, reaching millions of mainstream consumers who had never listened to electronic music before. Its rhythmic, sampled bases influenced many pop and mainstream artists, establishing Moby as a visionary who redefined electronic music's role in popular culture. "el primer legado que dejaría movi con este disco es que habría a los Estados Unidos a un nuevo campo de electrónica más pausada y más ambiental."
